title: Labor Department's H-1B Investigations Surge 48% as Project Firewall Targets Tech Employers
excerpt: The DOL initiative has launched nearly 200 probes and assessed millions in back wages, shifting from complaint-driven reviews to proactive, AI-powered investigations.
body:
• The U.S. Labor Department's Project Firewall has driven a 48% increase in H-1B investigations since its September 2025 launch, with nearly 200 active probes targeting major tech employers.
  • The enforcement shift moves from complaint-driven reviews to proactive, AI-powered investigations that can expand from a single petition to full workforce audits of payroll, hiring, and job classifications.
  • DOL has assessed $15 million in back wages, with violating employers facing civil fines and potential debarment from the H-1B program — a critical concern for Indian workers who hold roughly 72% of approved H-1B petitions.
  • Companies are investing in H-1B compliance self-audits for the first time as enforcement coordination expands across DOL, USCIS, DOJ Civil Rights, and the EEOC.

A New Enforcement Model

The U.S. Department of Labor has fundamentally changed how it polices the H-1B visa program. Project Firewall, launched on September 19, 2025, has produced a 48% surge in the agency's H-1B investigative caseload, according to a DOL official cited by Bloomberg Law. The initiative has generated nearly 200 active investigations into companies suspected of misusing the specialty occupation visa program.

https://x.com/AymanMatNews/status/2096611556817568233

Unlike the DOL's traditional complaint-driven approach, Project Firewall uses data analytics and artificial intelligence to proactively identify employers for investigation. Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer has personally certified at least one probe, invoking a previously unused authority that allows the agency to launch broader investigations without waiting for an outside complaint.

"They're not focusing on just drugs and thugs anymore. They're looking for hyper-technical violations," immigration attorney Kevin Andrews told Bloomberg Law, adding that the government's AI capabilities are bringing "an extra level of seriousness" to enforcement.

Broader Scope, Deeper Audits

The shift extends well beyond volume. Immigration attorneys report a sharp increase in site visits and more complex, data-driven information requests from investigators. Probes that begin with a single worker's petition can now expand into full workforce audits examining payroll records, hiring practices, job roles, qualifications, and whether those details match filings with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

"The investigations that will come from secretarial certified compliance reviews will be broader in scope than complaint driven investigations."

— Edward Raleigh, Partner at Fragomen, Del Rey, Bernsen & Loewy

By November 2025, the DOL had assessed $15 million in back wages across its active probes, according to immigration news outlet VisaVerge. Employers found non-compliant face consequences including repayment of wages owed, civil monetary penalties, and debarment from the H-1B program entirely.

Enforcement targets include wage underpayment, failure to recruit U.S. workers in good faith, misrepresentation of job responsibilities, non-existent work sites listed on filings, and "benching" — failing to pay H-1B workers during periods without active assignments.

Multi-Agency Coordination

Project Firewall does not operate in isolation. The DOL is coordinating enforcement with the Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and USCIS, according to law firm Holland & Knight. This layered structure means a wage complaint at DOL could trigger parallel inquiries into immigration fraud at USCIS or discriminatory hiring at DOJ, significantly multiplying legal exposure for employers.

The initiative targets the H-1B program's heaviest users, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta Platforms. But smaller IT consulting and staffing firms — many of which are Indian-owned and rely heavily on placing workers at third-party client sites — face equal if not greater vulnerability given their dependence on the program.

What It Means for Indian H-1B Workers

The enforcement escalation carries particular weight for the Indian diaspora. Indians account for approximately 72% of approved H-1B applications, and Indian IT consulting firms have historically relied on the program's provisions for deploying workers to client locations — a model now under intense regulatory scrutiny.

The pressure is already reshaping how companies approach H-1B hiring. Employers are investing in compliance self-audits of their H-1B documentation for the first time, according to Bloomberg Law, as the risk of enforcement has moved from theoretical to active.

H-1B employer registrations have already declined sharply. Roughly 344,000 employers registered for visas in 2025, down more than 25% from 2024 and less than half the 759,000 registered in 2023, according to Reuters. While multiple factors contribute — including a proposed $103,265 supplemental fee for cap-subject petitions and new wage-based lottery rules — the enforcement climate under Project Firewall has added urgency to the compliance burden.

What's Next

The DOL's enforcement trajectory shows no signs of slowing. For H-1B employers, the takeaway is direct: maintain meticulous records, ensure wage classifications match actual job duties, and prepare for the possibility of unannounced audits that extend beyond the scope of any single petition. Immigration attorneys are advising clients to conduct internal compliance reviews proactively — before investigators come knocking.
nri_angle: Indian H-1B workers and IT consulting firms face heightened enforcement risk as DOL's Project Firewall expands proactive investigations targeting wage violations and job misclassification.
